questions.stem: How does sexual reproduction restore the diploid chromosome number?

options.text: Two haploid gametes fuse during fertilization to form a diploid zygote
options.why: Each gamete supplies one chromosome from every homologous pair. Their fusion restores two chromosome sets.

options.text: A diploid gamete divides by mitosis to produce a haploid zygote
options.why: The chromosome numbers are reversed here. Gametes are haploid, while the zygote formed by their fusion is diploid.

options.text: Homologous chromosomes duplicate during fertilization inside each gamete
options.why: Chromosomes aren't duplicated to restore diploidy. One haploid set arrives in each of the two gametes.

options.text: Two diploid gametes exchange alleles and produce a diploid zygote
options.why: Gametes produced by meiosis are haploid, not diploid. Fusion of two diploid cells would double the normal chromosome number.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes genotype from phenotype?

options.text: Genotype is an organism’s allele combination, while phenotype is its observable traits
options.why: Genotype names the inherited alleles. Phenotype is the observable result of genotype, environment and their interaction.

options.text: Genotype is an observable characteristic, while phenotype is the DNA sequence producing it
options.why: Those definitions are backwards. Observable traits are phenotypes, while inherited allele combinations are genotypes.

options.text: Genotype includes environmental effects, while phenotype contains inherited information only
options.why: Environmental effects contribute to phenotype. They don't become part of the organism’s inherited genotype.

options.text: Genotype describes dominant alleles, while phenotype describes recessive alleles in an organism
options.why: Both dominant and recessive alleles belong to the genotype. Phenotype describes the traits produced, not one allele category.

questions.stem: A genetically identical plant develops broad leaves in shade and narrow leaves in bright light. What best explains this observation?

options.text: Environmental conditions altered gene expression without changing the plant’s genotype
options.why: This is phenotypic plasticity. One genotype produces different phenotypes as environmental conditions alter gene expression.

options.text: Bright light created a targeted mutation for narrow leaves in every plant cell
options.why: Phenotypic plasticity doesn't require a mutation. Environmental effects can change gene expression while the DNA sequence remains unchanged.

options.text: The plant inherited different alleles after it was moved into bright light
options.why: An individual doesn't inherit a new allele when its environment changes. Inheritance occurred when the zygote formed.

options.text: A recessive leaf allele became dominant because the light intensity increased
options.why: Dominance relationships don't switch when light changes. The environment affected expression of the existing genotype.

questions.stem: Which parental genotypes could produce children with blood groups A, B, AB and O?

options.text: I^Ai and I^Bi
options.why: These parents can produce I^AI^B, I^Ai, I^Bi and ii, giving all four blood-group phenotypes.

options.text: I^AI^A and I^BI^B
options.why: Every child would inherit I^A from one parent and I^B from the other, so every child would have blood group AB.

options.text: I^AI^B and ii
options.why: This cross produces I^Ai or I^Bi, so the children can have blood group A or B but not AB or O.

options.text: I^Ai and ii
options.why: This cross produces I^Ai or ii, so only blood groups A and O are possible.

questions.stem: Which genotype represents a male with haemophilia?

options.text: X^hY
options.why: A male has one X chromosome, so the recessive haemophilia allele on that X is expressed.

options.text: X^HX^h
options.why: This represents a heterozygous female carrier. The dominant unaffected allele usually masks the recessive haemophilia allele.

options.text: X^hY^h
options.why: The haemophilia allele is written on the X chromosome. The Y chromosome isn't assigned a corresponding allele.

options.text: X^HY
options.why: This represents an unaffected male because his X chromosome carries the unaffected allele.

questions.stem: Two unaffected parents have a child with a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Which parental genotypes fit this observation?

options.text: Both parents are heterozygous carriers
options.why: Each unaffected parent can carry one recessive allele. The affected child can inherit one recessive allele from each.

options.text: Both parents are homozygous dominant
options.why: Two homozygous dominant parents have no recessive allele to pass to the child.

options.text: One parent is homozygous dominant and one is heterozygous
options.why: The homozygous dominant parent always supplies a dominant allele, so an affected homozygous recessive child can't result.

options.text: Both parents are homozygous recessive but show no symptoms
options.why: For the stated inheritance pattern, homozygous recessive individuals are affected rather than unaffected carriers.

questions.stem: In a box-and-whisker analysis, Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 20. Which value would be classified as an upper outlier?

options.why: The IQR is 8, so the upper fence is 20 + 1.5 × 8 = 32. A value of 33 lies above it.
The upper outlier fence is 32. A value of 31 lies below that boundary.
A value of 24 is within 1.5 interquartile ranges above Q3, so it isn't an upper outlier.
This is Q3 itself, the upper edge of the box, rather than an outlier.

questions.stem: Why can alleles of two genes on different chromosomes assort independently?

options.text: Each homologous pair can orient independently at metaphase I of meiosis
options.why: The orientation of one homologous pair doesn't determine another pair’s orientation. This creates different chromosome combinations in gametes.

options.text: Sister chromatids from every chromosome pair separate independently during prophase I
options.why: Sister chromatids normally remain joined during prophase I. Independent orientation concerns homologous pairs at metaphase I.

options.text: Every allele crosses over to a chromosome from a different homologous pair
options.why: Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of one homologous pair, not between unrelated chromosomes.

options.text: Each gene mutates independently before homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis
options.why: Independent assortment comes from chromosome orientation and separation, not from mutation.

questions.stem: What phenotypic ratio is expected from AaBb × aabb when both genes are unlinked and show complete dominance?

options.why: The heterozygote produces four gamete types equally, while the double-recessive parent produces only ab gametes.
That ratio is expected from crossing two dihybrid heterozygotes, AaBb × AaBb, under the same assumptions.
That is the usual phenotypic ratio for a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, not this dihybrid test cross.
That is the genotypic ratio at one locus in a heterozygote cross. It doesn't describe the four phenotypes here.

questions.stem: Why do two closely linked autosomal genes produce more parental gametes than recombinant gametes?

options.text: The loci travel together unless a crossover occurs between them
options.why: Linked alleles stay on the same chromosome unless crossing over separates them. Crossovers between nearby loci occur in only some meioses.

options.text: Parental gametes survive because recombinant gametes always carry harmful mutations
options.why: Recombinant gametes don't necessarily contain mutations or harmful alleles. Their lower frequency comes from how often crossing over occurs between the loci.

options.text: Linked genes occupy the same locus and therefore cannot separate during meiosis
options.why: Different linked genes occupy different loci on the same chromosome. A crossover between those loci can separate their allele combinations.

options.text: The dominant alleles attract each other and enter the same gamete during meiosis
options.why: Dominance affects phenotype, not chromosome movement. Physical positions on a chromosome cause linkage.

questions.stem: A heterozygote has linked alleles in the arrangement AB/ab and is crossed with ab/ab. Which offspring are recombinant classes?

options.text: Aabb and aaBb
options.why: These offspring reveal Ab and aB gametes from the heterozygote, which differ from its parental AB and ab combinations.

options.text: AaBb and aabb
options.why: These offspring reveal the parental AB and ab gametes. They retain the combinations present on the heterozygote’s homologs.

options.text: AABB and aabb
options.why: AABB can't be produced because the tester contributes only ab. The aabb class is possible, but it is parental.

options.text: AaBB and AAbb
options.why: The ab/ab tester can't supply a B or A allele, so neither genotype can be produced in this cross.

questions.stem: A chi-squared test of four dihybrid phenotype classes gives p = 0.02. What conclusion is appropriate at the 0.05 significance level?

options.text: Reject the null hypothesis because the observed difference is statistically significant
options.why: A p value below 0.05 means the observed departure would be unlikely under the null hypothesis. The data may support linkage.

options.text: Fail to reject the null hypothesis because 0.02 is below the significance level
options.why: A p value below the chosen significance level leads to rejection, not failure to reject.

options.text: Accept the null hypothesis because some observed and expected values are different
options.why: Observed values normally differ from expected values. The chi-squared result evaluates whether the total difference is larger than chance reasonably explains.

options.text: Conclude that linkage has been proved because the p value is below 0.05
options.why: The result supports a significant departure from independent assortment, but it doesn't prove that linkage is the only possible cause.
